title: Torque: Nm vs lb-ft, and Why Your Wrench Is Probably Miscalibrated
h1: Torque conversion — N·m, lb·ft, kgf·m and wrench accuracy
description: 1 N·m = 0.737562 lb·ft. Wheel lugs typically 120–140 N·m (89–103 lb·ft). Click wrenches drift 4% per year — ISO 6789 requires recalibration every 5000 cycles or 12 months.

hero: One Newton-metre is 0.737562 pound-feet. That's the easy part. The hard part is that a click-style torque wrench loses roughly 4% accuracy per year in normal shop use — so the fastener you 'torqued to spec' may be 15% low or 20% high, and you'll never know until something backs out or snaps.
body: Torque is a rotational analogue of force: **τ = r × F**, distance times perpendicular force. In SI it is measured in Newton-metres (N·m). Because torque and energy share the same dimension (kg·m²/s²), the SI Brochure (BIPM, 9th ed. §2.3.4) explicitly forbids expressing torque in joules — 'to distinguish it from energy, torque should be given in N·m, never J' — even though they're dimensionally identical.
## The exact factors

> 1 N·m = 0.737562149 lb·ft (pound-force · foot)
> 1 N·m = 8.85074579 lb·in
> 1 lb·ft = 1.35581795 N·m
> 1 kgf·m = 9.80665 N·m = 7.23301 lb·ft
> 1 oz·in = 0.00706155 N·m (used for small motors and instrument screws)
## Common fastener torques

| Fastener | Typical torque | Note |
|---|---|---|
| M6 8.8 steel bolt, dry | 10 N·m (7.4 lb·ft) | Bosch table |
| M8 8.8 dry | 24 N·m (17.7 lb·ft) | |
| M10 8.8 dry | 47 N·m (34.7 lb·ft) | |
| M12 8.8 dry | 81 N·m (59.7 lb·ft) | |
| M14 8.8 dry | 128 N·m (94.4 lb·ft) | |
| M16 8.8 dry | 197 N·m (145 lb·ft) | |
| Passenger-car wheel lug | 108–140 N·m (80–103 lb·ft) | Model-specific; check owner's manual |
| Spark plug (14 mm, gasket) | 25–35 N·m (18–26 lb·ft) | NGK spec |
| Bicycle stem M5 bolt | 5 N·m (44 lb·in) | Never guess — carbon splits |
| MacBook trackpad screw | 0.16 N·m (1.4 lb·in) | iFixit spec |

For bolts, torque is a **proxy for clamp load** (preload). The relationship is τ = K · d · F, where K ≈ 0.20 for dry threads, 0.15 for lubricated, and d is nominal diameter. Lubricating a bolt with anti-seize and torquing to the dry spec **over-tightens by ~30%** — a common cause of stripped threads and stretched studs.
## Wrench accuracy — ISO 6789
ISO 6789-1:2017 classifies torque wrenches by accuracy tolerance:

> Class A: fixed-value indicating (dial/electronic), ±4% of reading
> Class B: adjustable click, ±4% (≥10% of full scale), ±6% (<10% of FS)
> Class C: adjustable click without scale, ±6%
> Requirement: recalibrate every 5000 operations OR 12 months, whichever comes first

A Snap-On or Proto click wrench meets Class B when new. Storage tips: back the adjustment off to the lowest setting (not zero — that unloads the spring completely and can lose zero calibration). A wrench used daily in a body shop typically drifts to ±10% by month 18 without service. Beam-type wrenches (the simple scale-and-pointer design) hold ±3% indefinitely because there is no spring to fatigue.
## Torque wrench technique — the 5 rules

1. **Pull perpendicular** to the handle. A 10° off-axis pull reduces effective torque by 1.5% (cos 10°).
2. **Grip at the marked pivot point.** Extending your grip toward the head reduces applied torque; the wrench calibrates against a specific lever length.
3. **Two-stage tighten:** snug to 50–60% of final spec, then torque to final in one smooth motion. Stop at first click — a second click adds another 3–5%.
4. **Torque + angle for critical joints.** Modern engine bolts (head, main bearing, con-rod) are 'torque to yield' — e.g., 'M11 × 55 mm: 30 N·m + 90° + 90°'. The angle stretches the bolt into its plastic region, guaranteeing preload independent of thread friction. These bolts are single-use.
5. **Never use a click wrench to *loosen*.** The ratchet mechanism doesn't damage, but a stuck fastener can spike torque well above the wrench's rated range and knock it out of calibration.
## Extension math
Adding a crow's-foot or straight extension in-line with the wrench axis: **no change to torque reading**. Adding an offset (a crow's-foot at 90° to the wrench body) changes the effective lever arm:

> τ_actual = τ_indicated × (L + E) / L
> where L = wrench length (handle to drive), E = extension offset
> Or the reverse: to apply 100 N·m through a 100 mm crow's-foot on a 450 mm wrench, set the wrench to 100 × 450 / (450 + 100) = 82 N·m.
## Worked example — cylinder head bolts
Toyota 2AR-FE 2.5L four-cylinder head bolt spec: **49 N·m + 90°**. In lb·ft: 49 × 0.737562 = 36.1 lb·ft. Sequence:

> 1. Lubricate threads and under-head with engine oil (Toyota spec).
> 2. Torque all 10 bolts to 36 lb·ft in the factory pattern.
> 3. Angle-turn each 90° in the same pattern.
> 4. Bolts are torque-to-yield — replace with new on every disassembly.
Under-torque risks a blown head gasket; over-torque snaps the bolt in the block. Neither is recoverable without pulling the engine.
## kgf·m — the third unit

Japanese factory manuals still list torque in kgf·m (kilogram-force metres): '5.0 kgf·m' means 5.0 × 9.80665 = 49.03 N·m = 36.2 lb·ft. Older Italian, French, and Soviet manuals do the same. Do not confuse **kg·m** (the same thing, sloppily written) with the SI kg·m/s of momentum. If a spec sheet says '9.5 kg-m' for a spark plug, it's 93 N·m and something has been mistyped — no plug takes that.
## The five-second recap

N·m × 0.7376 = lb·ft. Torque wrenches drift — recalibrate yearly. Lubricated threads take 30% less torque than dry for the same preload. Torque-to-yield bolts are single-use. Never write torque in joules.

faqs.q: Do I need to convert if my wrench reads only in lb·ft and the spec is in N·m?
faqs.a: Divide N·m by 1.356 to get lb·ft (or use the converter). Set the wrench to the converted value; do not try to interpolate between marks.

In engineering, torque is properly pound-foot (lb·ft), and foot-pound (ft·lb) is a unit of energy. In practice, US shops and tool catalogues use 'ft-lb' for torque everywhere. Numerically identical; pedantically distinct.

faqs.q: Can I extend a torque wrench with a pipe?
faqs.a: No — you invalidate the calibration and risk over-torque. Use a longer wrench or a torque multiplier (planetary gearbox) with its own calibration certificate.

faqs.q: Why do bike shops all use 5 N·m for stem bolts?
faqs.a: Carbon components have a narrow safe range (typically 4–6 N·m). Under-torque means the bar slips; over-torque cracks the clamp. Every Park Tool ATD-1 preset wrench is fixed at 5 N·m for exactly this reason.

faqs.q: How is torque measured on a dyno?
faqs.a: The engine drives an eddy-current or water brake that resists rotation. A load cell on the brake arm measures force at a known radius; torque = force × radius. Power is computed from τ × ω, not measured directly.
